connector: Chapter 10 ended with forty people free and Harriet saying, “My people must go free.” In Chapter 11 she goes back for her brothers, who are about to be sold south. In Chapter 12 the people in danger are her old parents. Follow the chain: each problem, what Harriet does about it, and what that makes possible.

a.raw: she moved swiftly through the night her parents traveled slowly behind her
a.fixed: She moved swiftly through the night. Her parents traveled slowly behind her.
a.why: Capital S starts the sentence; a period ends the first sentence; capital H starts the second. Swiftly and slowly are adverbs that tell how.

b.raw: old rit sang bravely at the jail ben listened closely to her song
b.fixed: Old Rit sang bravely at the jail. Ben listened closely to her song.
b.why: Capital O and R on Old Rit (a name); a period ends the first sentence; capital B on Ben (a name). Bravely and closely are adverbs that tell how.

fill1.h1: Squeeze a sponge with both hands. Which root means push?
fill1.why: press means push: com + press = push together.

fill2.h1: A cruel ruler pushes his people down hard. Which root means push?
fill2.why: press means push: op + press = push down hard.

fill3.h1: When you finally reach a goal, you get hold of it. Which root means hold?
fill3.why: tain means hold: at + tain = reach, get hold of.

fill4.h1: The police can keep a person from leaving. Which root means hold?
fill4.why: tain means hold: de + tain = hold back.

notes.wgrd: One cause leads to an effect, and that effect can cause something else. Follow the whole chain, link by link, and say ‘so then’ between each one.
vocab: The act of ending something, especially slavery.
A guide on the Underground Railroad; or, the person who runs a train.
To make a thought, feeling, or idea known to others.
notes.wordParts: press means “push” and tain means “hold”: express, impress, contain, obtain.
notes.grammar: An adverb works with a verb. Find the verb first, then ask how, when, or where it happened.
notes.spelling: The suffixes -ive, -al, and -ic turn a word into a describing word: act → active, music → musical, hero → heroic. Look at the base word first. Sometimes a letter drops, like a silent e.

catcher.intro: As you read Ch. 11 and 12, write the links in order.

end.label: The link that holds the chain together

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: pushing, or holding?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, finishes a patchwork quilt, the family’s only treasure. Years later, in Chapter 12, Harriet tucks that same quilt over her parents’ legs as she drives them out of slavery. press means push, and tain means hold. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: Old Rit’s quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. press = push, tain = hold.

ft.songsIntro: In Chapter 12, Old Ben is in jail, and the sheriff never leaves him alone. Harriet has come to get him out, and he has to be ready. So Harriet tells Old Rit how to carry the message, and Old Rit sings.

songs.title: Good News, the Chariot’s Coming
lines: An’ I don’t want it to leave me behind.
songs.heard: A church song about the chariot that carries people home to heaven. The sheriff hears an old woman singing a hymn.
songs.meant: Harriet is here, and she has come to take Ben out. He understands and mouths one word: When?
songs.q: The sheriff is standing right there. Why does Old Rit sing the message instead of saying it?
songs.a: Saying it would give the plan away. A hymn was safe to sing, and Ben knew how to listen to it.

songs.title: Lovely Fan
lines: Then lovely Fan, will you come out tonight?
Then lovely Fan, will you come out tonight,
An’ dance by the light of the moon?
songs.heard: A silly old dance song, sung as the sheriff shoves Old Rit out the door.
songs.meant: Tonight. Be ready to come out tonight.
songs.q: Ben asked “When?” and there was no time to answer. How does this song answer him?
songs.a: Its words ask someone to come out tonight. That tells Ben the escape is tonight.
songs.source: An old dance song · public domain

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Two chapters today, and both are about Harriet’s own family. First her brothers, who are about to be sold. Then her mother and father, who are too old to walk north. Today’s question: what does Harriet do when the usual road to freedom won’t work?
transcripts.read: Track the chain as you read: a problem, what Harriet does, and what that leads to. Watch a letter that makes no sense to the postmaster, and a pair of chickens. In Chapter 12, listen to what Old Rit sings at the jail. On my tours, that part always got a laugh.
transcripts.spelling: These endings turn a word into a describing word. Here’s the tricky part. Some starting words end in a silent e, and that e drops off before the ending. Some lose nothing at all. So don’t trust your ears. Look hard at the starting word, then build.

virtue.title: Helping someone get free?
virtue.intro: In Chapters 11 and 12, many people help, in big ways and small ones. Read each moment. Tap Helping someone get free or Not this time.

items.t: Harriet lets her chickens loose and chases them, so John Stewart won’t see her face.
items.why: Her trick keeps her hidden, so the rescue can go on.

items.t: Ben brings food to the fodder house with a handkerchief over his eyes, so he can say he never saw his children.
items.why: He feeds them and protects them, without telling a lie.

items.t: Old Rit and Ben fatten a pig all summer for a Christmas dinner.
items.why: That is love for their sons, but it is not part of the escape.

items.t: Jacob Jackson gives up his only horse so Ben and Old Rit can ride.
items.why: He gives the thing he worked years for, so they can get away.

items.t: The sheriff tells his wife that Ben laughs as if he’d come into a fortune.
items.why: The sheriff doesn’t understand what is happening at all.
